title: Enabling Differentially Private Federated Learning for Speech Recognition: Benchmarks, Adaptive Optimizers and Gradient Clipping

strengths: The proposed ASR benchmark addresses a useful problem with natural speaker-level partitions, substantial data heterogeneity, and domain shift between LibriSpeech and Common Voice. Experiments cover English, French, and German.

The empirical investigation is extensive: seed quality, cohort size, optimizers, normalization, local computation, augmentation, and FedProx are examined. Several seeded FL configurations approach centralized accuracy within 2,000 aggregation rounds, and transferring hyperparameters across languages strengthens the findings.

Per-layer clipping produces a substantial measured improvement: at matched noise and clipping bounds, English test WER improves from 31.1% with global clipping to 20.4% with dimension-based clipping. The method preserves the overall sensitivity bound, and its origin in prior work is appropriately acknowledged.

The appendices document preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, noise conventions, negative results, and compute costs. Public pretraining assumptions, extrapolated results, and diagnostic experiments without DP guarantees are explicitly identified; this transparency is valuable.
weaknesses: The central privacy–utility result is insufficiently validated. The measured 20.4% and 23.7% WER configurations have reported epsilon values around 1.2×10^8 and 1.1×10^7, respectively. Obtaining the headline epsilon values of 7.2 and 4.5 requires projecting to roughly 70 million and 7 million users, with cohorts of 204,800, while assuming unchanged utility. Although this assumption is disclosed, neither a scaling study nor a theoretical argument establishes it. Consequently, the claimed operating points remain projections rather than demonstrated private ASR capabilities.

The privacy analysis needs reconciliation with the actual mechanism. Algorithm 1 specifies Poisson sampling and normalization by the realized cohort size, while Theorem 1 uses sensitivity C/(qN); the implementation instead fixes the cohort size. These choices do not automatically correspond to the same sampled-Gaussian accountant. The exact sampling, normalization, and adjacency assumptions should be justified together. Table 2 also reports epsilon values of 1.3 and 13 for identical z=1.024, q, T, and delta, indicating an accounting-table error.

The proposed explanation is not fully aligned with the ablations. The abstract and main text emphasize noise overwhelming attention parameters, whereas Appendix D.5 identifies MLP parameters as the dominant source of degradation. Per-layer clipping also gives only marginal improvements for French and German. These results support a narrower, configuration-dependent insight rather than the broad claim that this remedy is essential for large transformer ASR.

Practical cross-device feasibility is not established by limiting aggregation rounds alone. Full training and communication of a 255M-parameter model, especially with projected cohorts exceeding 200,000 devices, require evidence about device memory, bandwidth, availability, and latency. GPU simulation costs are reported, but they do not substantiate the deployment or low-resource-language claims.

The claim of nearly optimal FL without pretraining is too broad. In Table 4, the largest evaluated cohort trained from scratch on Common Voice English obtains 25.7% test WER versus 18.2% centrally, a substantial 7.5-point gap. The strongest conclusions should distinguish seeded adaptation from training from scratch.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite detailed appendices: code is only promised, exact randomized speaker partitions are not supplied, and repeated-run uncertainty is not reported. This particularly limits assessment of the smaller optimizer and clipping improvements and reuse of the proposed benchmark.
